newsitem.title: SPAIN: FOCUS-Spain grows 2.2 percent, rate cuts still seen.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Spain grows 2.2 percent, rate cuts still seen.

text.p: Spain's economic growth accelerated in the fourth quarter to post an overall 2.2 percent expansion in 1996, but economists said on Wednesday the rise would not threaten expected interest rate cuts this year.
Gross domestic product expanded at a 2.6 percent rate in the fourth-quarter over the year-ago quarter and at a 0.8 percent rate from the third quarter for a total 2.2 percent 1996 growth.
"In the last quarter, growth was higher than 2.5 percent. These data are making more likely government forecasts for 1997," said Economy Secretary Cristobal Montoro.
The government forecast real growth of 2.3 percent for 1996 and of three percent for 1997.
Although the 1996 figure was slightly beneath the government's forecast, it was a bit better than the market had foreseen although the effect on financial markets was limited.
"The data are good, a little bit better than we expected," said Alfredo Urrutia, economist at Societe Generale in Madrid.
But economists said the growth was not strong enough to hamper the Bank of Spain from further lowering interest rates.
The central bank has cut its key interest rate to a current six percent from nine percent at the start of 1996 amid a sharp fall in the inflation rate and fiscal belt-tightening measures.
Inflation fell to a 28-year low of 2.9 percent in January.
The government has pledged to cut the deficit to just three percent of GDP this year from 4.4 percent last year and from 6.6 percent in 1995.
Economic growth was boosted by robust exports, which expanded a real 12.1 percent in the final quarter of last year.
"This sector is giving key signs of strength that point to the competitiveness of the Spanish economy," said Valentin Fernandez, economist at Credit Lyonnais in Madrid.
Carmen Hernansanz, economist at Merrill Lynch in Madrid, said the data showed overall the economy had rebounded from a sluggish period that began in 1995.

"In principle, it seems we've got over the transitory slump in the last phase of 1995 and the first part of 1996. (But) GDP components are not going to stop the Bank of Spain from cutting rates," Hernansanz said.
Some analysts were sceptical that Spain could reach its 1997 goal despite the late improvement last year.
"Overall, we see 2.4 percent for 1997. We will improve, but it's still a far shot from the government's three-percent forecast," said Henrik Lumholdt, economist at Bank of America in Madrid.
Exports are unlikely to increase and private consumption should remain steady, he said. Capital goods growth could lose vitality, although construction should rebound.
But Colin Warren, economist at Tokai Bank in London, said the data showed the economy was certainly not on the verge of recession and therefore the Bank of Spain need be in no rush to lower rates.
"With fairly high growth, a weak peseta and a very tough target for inflation in 1998, I don't think the Bank of Spain should feel any urgency to cut rates," Warren said.
